newsitem.title: UK: Nigeria's gasoline appetite in Med seen resurfacin.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria's gasoline appetite in Med seen resurfacin.

text.p: Nigeria, noticeably absent from the Mediterranean gasoline market in the last few months, is expected to step up its products purchases very soon as traders bet that its refineries will not be able to hold out at their higher utilisation rates.

But Med supplies remain very tight and fresh Nigerian demand may suck cargoes out of Northwest Europe, which is flush with extra supply after the arbitrage to the United States was closed earlier this month, they said.
Market rumours and unconfirmed Nigerian press reports said two of the four refineries had cut throughput, either because of maintenance or glitches, but this could not be confirmed.
Refinery officials had already announced scheduled maintenance for the year at some plants.
"Inventories in Nigeria are critically low," one trader in London said. "They need to make a decision relatively shortly and when they come out, there is no gasoline in the Med to buy."

Nigeria, an OPEC producer of about 2.10 million barrels per day, normally imports gasoline to meet its domestic consumption because its refineries operate below capacity and are plagued by poor management and spare parts shortages, traders said.
But its four refineries have run at relatively high utilisation rates since the fourth quarter and cut its needs for gasoline imports, traders said.
The four refineries were processing about 250,000 barrels per day from a theoretical capacity of 445,000 bpd after reaching 75 percent of capacity in November, according to oil ministry officials.
It historically bought up to five to 10 cargoes a month, mostly of lower octane cat gas, with at least two to three coming from the Mediterranean, either from Spain or France, traders said.

"In November, December, January and February the Nigerians have not purchased a cargo of gasoline and it put an enormous amount of pressure on the Med," the trader said. "The story is that the Med was weak but it has turned around."

The 110,000 bpd Kaduna plant was expected to close for maintenance in the first or second quarter, and the 150,000 bpd Port Harcourt New Refinery to shut in the fourth quarter, according to refinery officials.
No maintenance was planned at Warri's 125,000 bpd refinery but rumours surfaced that the it had to cut throughput, traders said. This was not confirmed.
Speculation also circulated that the Port Harcourt refinery was down last week and starting to step up throughput, but this was also unconfirmed.

"If I was a betting man, which I am in this business, I would say that they are not going to last full time for much longer so I would expect them...to come back (into the market)," another trader said.
"They will want to keep the refineries running through summer, so it would be likely they would have some maintenance before that," he said.
Nigerian demand could not have come at a tighter time for the Med, where turnarounds in Italy and Greece exacerbated the robust demand from Lebanon, the Black Sea and Italy, traders said.
The arbitrage to the United States also vacuumed material out of the Med in January and February. The arb from NWE to the Med was not profitable yet due to high shipping costs, traders said.
The Middle East scooped up 400,000 tonnes of gasoline from Northwest Europe and the Med in February, a trader estimated.

Another trader said much of the cat gas normally bought by Nigeria was scooped up by the U.S. and Argentina. A 60,000 tonne gasoline cargo had already moved from NWE to the Med and possibly on to the Middle East, and another one was likley following it, he said.
"If the refineries stay up, they should not be major buyers...The key there is the refineries," he said.
